ai.definition: Fusion Energy is a technology that aims to harness the power of nuclear fusion, the process that powers stars like the sun. In this process, light nuclei (such as isotopes of hydrogen) are heated to extremely high temperatures to form plasma, which is then confined using magnetic or inertial methods until they fuse, releasing vast amounts of energy.
ai.howItWorks: Fusion involves heating hydrogen isotopes (deuterium and tritium) to millions of degrees Celsius to create a plasma state. This plasma is then contained using either magnetic confinement in devices like tokamaks or inertial confinement in lasers or z-pinch machines until the nuclei are close enough to fuse, releasing energy through the conversion of mass into energy according to Einstein's equation E=mc^2.
ai.problemSolved: Fusion Energy addresses the need for a sustainable and virtually limitless source of clean energy. It promises to provide baseload power with minimal environmental impact compared to fossil fuels or fission-based nuclear reactors, which could help mitigate climate change and reduce dependence on non-renewable resources.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing fusion devices is complex due to the high temperatures and precise conditions required for plasma confinement and control. Materials must withstand extreme heat and radiation, making production challenging and expensive.
ai.buildProcess: The build process involves designing, constructing, and testing large-scale fusion reactors such as tokamaks or stellarators over many years. This includes developing advanced materials, improving plasma confinement techniques, and optimizing energy conversion systems.
ai.costDrivers: High initial capital costs for infrastructure, ongoing research and development expenses, and the need for specialized materials that can withstand extreme conditions are significant cost drivers in fusion energy projects.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook for commercialization is uncertain but promising. While several prototypes have been tested, scaling up to a commercially viable reactor remains challenging.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks for fusion energy are still being developed as the technology moves from lab-scale experiments to larger scale demonstrations and eventual commercial deployment. Safety standards and environmental regulations will need to be established.
ai.risks: Technical risks include achieving sustained plasma conditions, maintaining long-term stability, and developing materials that can withstand extreme temperatures and radiation. Economic risks involve high initial investment costs and the potential for cost overruns in development projects.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently uncertain due to the early stage of commercialization and significant R&D investments required before any revenue streams are generated from energy production.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments will focus on improving confinement techniques, reducing costs, and scaling up reactor designs. Advances in materials science, plasma physics, and engineering could accelerate progress towards a commercially viable fusion power plant.

glossary.def: A state of matter consisting of ions and free electrons, often created by heating gases to very high temperatures.
A toroidal-shaped device used for magnetic confinement of plasma in nuclear fusion research.
A method of achieving nuclear fusion by compressing and heating a target containing fuel using intense lasers or particle beams.

subsystems.name: Confinement system
subsystems.role: keeps the fusing plasma away from any solid surface, either with strong magnetic fields or by crushing tiny fuel pellets with beams.
parts: magnet coils (magnetic route) or laser and beam drivers (inertial route)

subsystems.name: Fuel cycle
subsystems.role: supplies deuterium and tritium and recovers unburned tritium from the exhaust so it can be reused.

subsystems.name: Blanket and first wall
subsystems.role: absorbs the fusion neutrons, converts their energy into heat and breeds fresh tritium from lithium.

subsystems.name: Heat and power conversion
subsystems.role: moves blanket heat to a turbine and generator, much like a conventional thermal power station.

subsystems.name: Exhaust and vacuum
subsystems.role: removes helium ash and surplus heat and keeps the chamber at high vacuum.
parts: tritium recovery from the exhaust stream

subsystems.name: Remote handling and containment
subsystems.role: lets a plant be maintained without people entering, and keeps radioactive tritium from escaping.

buildSteps.title: Choose a confinement route
buildSteps.detail: Design the plant around either magnetic confinement (tokamak, stellarator) or inertial confinement driven by lasers or pulsed beams. The choice sets almost every other engineering decision.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the vacuum chamber
buildSteps.detail: Weld or bolt the chamber together in sections to tight tolerances, with hundreds of ports for heating, fuelling and instruments.

buildSteps.title: Install the confinement hardware
buildSteps.detail: For magnetic designs, wind superconducting coils and enclose them in a cryostat cooled to a few degrees above absolute zero. For inertial designs, build and align the beam drivers and the target chamber.

buildSteps.title: Line the interior
buildSteps.detail: Fit the lithium-bearing breeding blanket and the exhaust surfaces, and place neutron shielding between the plasma and the magnets or sensitive equipment.

buildSteps.title: Add fuel and vacuum plant
buildSteps.detail: Install deuterium injection, tritium processing, cryopumps and the tritium accounting systems that track every gram.

buildSteps.title: Condition and ignite the plasma
buildSteps.detail: Start on hydrogen to learn control, move to deuterium, then introduce tritium. Heat to roughly 100–150 million °C so nuclei overcome their mutual repulsion and fuse.

buildSteps.title: Sustain the burn and breed fuel
buildSteps.detail: Run long enough for neutrons to heat the blanket and breed tritium, so the plant produces its own fuel rather than consuming a stockpile.

buildSteps.title: Generate and export electricity
buildSteps.detail: Carry blanket heat to heat exchangers, raise steam, spin a turbine and feed the grid — while proving remote maintenance and safe tritium containment.

prerequisites.tech: Net energy gain in a confined plasma
prerequisites.why: laser fusion at the US National Ignition Facility released more energy than the laser delivered to the target in December 2022, but no magnetic device has yet produced more fusion energy than it consumes.
tritium barely exists in nature and decays with a 12.3-year half-life, so a power plant must manufacture its own from lithium; no integrated breeding blanket has yet produced net tritium.
fusion neutrons displace atoms in steel and other structures far faster than fission neutrons, and no material has been qualified for years of plant-level exposure.
coils wound from rare-earth barium copper oxide tape have reached around 20 tesla, enabling smaller and cheaper magnetic machines, but reliable industrial-scale production is still being proven.

prerequisites.tech: Steady-state plasma control and disruption avoidance
prerequisites.why: a power plant must run for hours or days, while today's devices typically run for seconds to minutes, and uncontrolled disruptions can damage the machine.
tritium is radioactive and permeates materials, so plants must be serviced by robots and keep releases close to zero.

pathway.milestone: ITER is being assembled in France, private ventures are building compact high-field tokamaks and alternative designs, and laser fusion has reached ignition
pathway.unlocks: the physics and engineering base needed to attempt a burning plasma.

pathway.milestone: a magnetic device shows more fusion energy out than heating energy in, running repeatedly rather than as a one-off shot
pathway.unlocks: confidence that net gain is achievable in a practical, repeatable machine.

pathway.milestone: pilot plants close the fuel cycle: breed tritium, tolerate neutron damage and produce hundreds of megawatts of heat
pathway.unlocks: the parts still missing between a physics experiment and a power station.

pathway.milestone: grid-connected demonstration plants, then commercial fleets
pathway.unlocks: firm, low-carbon baseload power with fuel drawn from seawater and lithium.
